text.p: The following are the main stories from Tuesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Pensions to fall to 64 percent of net salary from 70 percent by 2030
- Hamburg mayor Voscherau argues for more liberal policy towards heroin addicts
- Fresh controversy over German-Czech parliamentary declaration
- Germany denies that Foreign Minister Kinkel apologised to Turkish Foreign Minister Ciller over judge's comments
- Unions reject tax reform plan
- EU finance ministers want to undermine tax havens
- Official charged with embezzlement of Treuhand privatisation body
- Cartel Office says health insurers are subject to competition law
HANDELSBLATT
- Level of pensions to fall to 64 percent by 2030
- Electronics and engineering industry associations plan to merge
- Thyssen determined to push on with Transrapid train, denies rumour on merging rolled steel operations with Krupp KFHG.F
- Thyssen sees better return by year 2000 from new portfolio structure
- Private households slow to buy personal computers
- Finance minister Waigel urges fair tax competition, wants to combat tax havens
- Siemens gets big order from China National Technical Import and Export Corp
- Lufthansa load factor declines
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Level of pensions to fall to 64 percent
- DGB and SPD caution that tax reform may cause social unrest
- Parliament remembers Holocaust victims
- Baden-Wuerttemberg state to try out "quickie-trials" for minor criminals
- Hamburg mayor Voscherau wants supervised heroin distribution for addicts
- Bonn wants to combat tax havens in EU
- Winter sales make brisk start
- Savings banks complain about cost of harmonisation
- Steel production rises
- Property funds are hit of 1996
- West German inflation 1.8 percent
DIE WELT
- Level of pensions to fall to 64 percent
- Autopsy to establish cause of death of possible BSE victim
- Bundestag remembers victims of Nazism
- Report criticises opposition SPD leadership structure
- Tax reform plans in the crossfire
- Pensions reform commission wants to introduce "family fund"
- Bonn savings plan to save social security providers and employers 150 billion marks between 1997 and 2000
- Many firms refusing to pay minimum wages
- Wrangling continues over size and powers of future postal regulation authority
- Unions angered by plan to tax overtime bonuses
